lessons.title: Diagnosing endometriosis with fertility in mind
lessons.objective: Approach diagnosis without routine laparoscopy (imaging, ultrasound limits, no biomarkers), recognise why empirical treatment does not fit when pregnancy is sought, and distinguish the rASRM stage from the EFI.
lessons.closing: Ultrasound first, no CA125 and no empirical contraceptive if she is trying to conceive; the stage describes anatomy and the EFI guides prognosis after surgery.

lessons.title: Surgery and hormone suppression when fertility is the priority
lessons.objective: Apply ESHRE and NICE recommendations on hormone suppression and on surgery for peritoneal, ovarian and deep disease, weighing the effect on ovarian reserve.
lessons.closing: Suppression does not improve fertility; surgery may help spontaneous pregnancy, but with endometrioma ovarian reserve must be weighed and in deep disease pain leads the decision.

lessons.title: IUI, IVF, preservation and complementary approaches
lessons.objective: Choose between IUI with stimulation and IVF, avoid pre-treatments and surgery without proven benefit before IVF, counsel on fertility preservation and explain what is known about diet and supplements.
lessons.closing: IVF works in endometriosis without long pre-treatment or routine surgery; preservation is discussed in extensive ovarian disease, and for diet and supplements the evidence is insufficient.

items.title: Imaging first: transvaginal ultrasound opens the work-up
items.core: ESHRE recommends using imaging (ultrasound or MRI) in the endometriosis work-up, bearing in mind that a negative result does not exclude it, particularly superficial peritoneal disease (strong recommendation, ⊕⊕). NICE offers transvaginal ultrasound to everyone with suspected endometriosis, even if the examination is normal (1.5.2), and asks not to exclude the disease if examination and ultrasound are normal (1.5.4). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
In the Cochrane review summarised by ESHRE, transvaginal ultrasound detects endometrioma well (sensitivity 93%, specificity 96%), but for superficial pelvic endometriosis its sensitivity is only 65%, with 95% specificity. For deep endometriosis, a meta-analysis gives transvaginal ultrasound 94% specificity and 79% sensitivity, and the Cochrane review gives MRI 77% and 94%. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

NICE justifies ultrasound because it identifies endometriomas and deep disease, rules out other pathology and guides management and referral (1.5.2). It suggests specialist ultrasound or MRI to diagnose deep endometriosis and assess its extent (1.5.9), and referral to a specialist centre if an endometrioma or deep disease is suspected or confirmed (1.5.6). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Which imaging test does NICE offer to everyone with suspected endometriosis, and what type of disease can it miss?
items.pearl: A normal scan does not mean “no endometriosis”: it makes an endometrioma unlikely but does not rule out superficial disease.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 5: strong, ⊕⊕. On ESHRE's GRADE scale, ⊕ = very low evidence, ⊕⊕ = low, ⊕⊕⊕ = moderate and ⊕⊕⊕⊕ = high; strength (strong/weak) and quality of evidence are different things. NICE NG73 1.5.2 [2024]; 1.5.4, 1.5.6 and 1.5.9 [2017, amended 2024].

items.title: Empirical treatment is contraceptive: it does not fit when she is trying to conceive
items.core: ESHRE considers both diagnostic laparoscopy and imaging plus empirical treatment (hormonal contraceptives or progestogens) acceptable, with no proven superiority of either, but frames empirical treatment for the patient who is not trying to conceive. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE notes that first-line hormonal treatment, such as the contraceptive pill, is not appropriate for people trying to conceive. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
In its 2012 committee opinion, ASRM stated that there is no evidence that medical treatment of endometriosis improves fertility and that fertility is essentially eliminated while it lasts, because all medical treatments inhibit ovulation. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]

NICE NG73 advises against offering hormonal treatment, alone or combined with surgery, to people trying to conceive, because it does not improve spontaneous pregnancy rates (1.10.4). It also asks for multidisciplinary management of endometriosis-related subfertility, with input from a fertility specialist. [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: Why does the “ultrasound + empirical contraceptive” approach not fit a patient who is trying to conceive?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: GDG statement (ungraded). NICE NG73 1.10.4 [2017, amended 2024]; NICE NG257, rationale for 1.36. ASRM 2012.

items.title: CA125 and other biomarkers do not diagnose endometriosis
items.core: ESHRE recommends against using biomarkers in endometrial tissue, blood, menstrual or uterine fluid to diagnose endometriosis (strong, ⊕⊕⊕), and NICE advises against using serum CA125 to diagnose it (1.5.8). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
In the meta-analysis cited by ESHRE, at a 30 U/ml threshold CA125 had 93% specificity but only 52% sensitivity for any endometriosis. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Examination does not settle the diagnosis either: ESHRE recommends it to identify deep nodules or endometriomas, although its diagnostic accuracy is low (strong, ⊕), and asks to proceed to imaging even if it is normal (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: What do ESHRE and NICE say about CA125 and other biomarkers to diagnose endometriosis?

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 4 strong, ⊕⊕⊕; rec. 2 strong, ⊕; rec. 3 strong, ⊕⊕. NICE NG73 1.5.8 [2017].

items.title: Diagnostic laparoscopy: when, and what to expect from it
items.core: ESHRE suggests considering laparoscopy for diagnosis and treatment if imaging is negative or empirical treatment failed or is inappropriate (GPP), and confirming lesions histologically, although negative histology does not entirely rule out the disease (GPP). NICE contemplates it even if ultrasound or MRI is normal (1.5.11). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
If a systematic laparoscopy, with normal and abnormal findings recorded and intra-operative imaging, is normal, NICE advises explaining that endometriosis is unlikely (1.5.15). During diagnostic laparoscopy, NICE suggests considering treatment of peritoneal disease not involving bowel, bladder or ureter and of uncomplicated endometriomas (1.9.4). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

ASRM (2012) considered laparoscopy of low utility in asymptomatic women with a normal ultrasound, because advanced disease is uncommon in them, and judged the benefit of treating minimal or mild endometriosis insufficient to recommend laparoscopy solely to increase the chance of pregnancy. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]
items.recall: In which situations does ESHRE suggest diagnostic laparoscopy, and what does ASRM think of doing it solely to improve fertility?
items.pearl: If you are doing a laparoscopy in a patient trying to conceive, agree with her beforehand what will be done if lesions are found.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 6 and 7, GPP. NICE NG73 1.5.11 and 1.5.15 [2017, amended 2024]; 1.9.4 [2017]. ASRM 2012.

items.title: rASRM stage and EFI: describing is not predicting
items.core: ESHRE notes there is no convincing correlation between disease extent by the rASRM classification and symptom severity, and that staging systems were designed mainly to describe extent and location for surgical purposes. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE advises treating according to symptoms, preferences and priorities rather than stage (1.6.1). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
For reproductive prognosis, ESHRE relies on the Endometriosis Fertility Index (EFI): an end-of-surgery score from 0 to 10 combining patient factors (age, duration of subfertility and prior pregnancy) and surgical factors (the “least function” score of tubes and ovaries and the rASRM lesion and total scores), which predicts non-ART pregnancy (natural conception or IUI) after surgery. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

According to ESHRE, the EFI has been externally validated in over 30 studies and is reproducible; it should be used to identify who will benefit from ART after surgery, taking into account other tests such as the partner's semen analysis (GDG statement), and the guideline notes that the index assumes normal gamete function. Estimating it before surgery to choose between surgery and ART has been studied in only one study. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: Which variables does the EFI combine, what does it predict and what does it assume?
items.pearl: A high EFI does not offset an abnormal semen analysis: the index assumes the gametes work.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: GDG statement on the EFI (ungraded). NICE NG73 1.6.1 [2017].

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman (fictional case) with severe dysmenorrhoea and deep dyspareunia has been trying to conceive for 14 months. Pelvic examination is normal. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start a continuous combined contraceptive as an empirical trial and reassess in 3 months.
options.why: ESHRE frames empirical treatment for those not trying to conceive; all medical treatments inhibit ovulation (ASRM 2012), and NICE considers it inappropriate when trying to conceive.

options.text: Transvaginal ultrasound, even though the examination is normal, and continue the couple’s fertility work-up.
options.why: Correct: NICE offers transvaginal ultrasound to everyone with suspected endometriosis even if examination is normal, and ESHRE recommends imaging even when the examination is normal.

options.text: Order CA125 to confirm the suspicion before any imaging.
options.why: NICE advises against CA125 to diagnose endometriosis and ESHRE recommends against biomarkers (strong).

options.text: Schedule a diagnostic laparoscopy directly without prior imaging.
options.why: NICE offers transvaginal ultrasound to everyone with suspected endometriosis (1.5.2) and, if deep disease is suspected, suggests considering specialist imaging before operative laparoscopy (1.5.12); ESHRE suggests laparoscopy after negative imaging or failed or inappropriate empirical treatment.

items.explanation: In someone trying to conceive, the work-up starts with ultrasound and fertility assessment; an empirical contraceptive is not a neutral option because it prevents conception.

items.stem: A woman with dysmenorrhoea and dyspareunia has a transvaginal ultrasound that is normal. According to the accuracy data reported by ESHRE, which statement is correct?

options.text: A normal ultrasound excludes endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE and NICE stress that a negative result does not exclude the disease, particularly superficial peritoneal disease.

options.text: It makes an endometrioma unlikely but does not rule out superficial peritoneal disease.
options.why: Correct: sensitivity is 93% for endometrioma but only 65% for superficial pelvic disease.

options.text: MRI is the test of choice to detect superficial peritoneal disease.
options.why: For pelvic endometriosis overall, no technique outperformed laparoscopy, and MRI showed low specificity and sensitivity (72% and 79%).

options.text: The next step should be CA125 to decide whether to investigate further.
options.why: CA125 has 52% sensitivity and NICE advises against using it to diagnose endometriosis.

items.explanation: Ultrasound is excellent for endometrioma and reasonable for deep disease, but blind to much superficial disease.

items.stem: Which of these statements about the Endometriosis Fertility Index (EFI) is correct according to ESHRE?

options.text: It is calculated from the preoperative ultrasound, and that use is widely validated.
options.why: It is an end-of-surgery score; estimating it before surgery has been studied in only one study.

options.text: It is a 0–10 end-of-surgery score that predicts non-ART pregnancy and assumes normal gamete function.
options.why: Correct: it combines patient and surgical factors and must be interpreted with other tests, such as the semen analysis.

options.text: It replaces the rASRM classification and uses none of its data.
options.why: The EFI incorporates the rASRM lesion and total scores.

options.text: It predicts the live-birth rate after IVF.
options.why: It predicts non-ART pregnancy (natural or with IUI); ESHRE uses it to identify who will benefit from ART.

items.explanation: The stage describes anatomy; the EFI helps decide whether, after surgery, to wait or move to ART.

items.title: Suppressing ovulation does not improve fertility
items.core: ESHRE recommends against prescribing ovarian suppression to improve fertility in infertile women with endometriosis (strong, ⊕⊕), and against postoperative hormone suppression solely to enhance pregnancy rates (strong, ⊕⊕). NICE advises against offering hormonal treatment, alone or combined with surgery, to people trying to conceive (1.10.4). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
If the woman cannot or does not want to try to conceive right after surgery, ESHRE allows offering hormone therapy, because it does not harm her fertility and improves the immediate effect of surgery on pain (weak, ⊕⊕). It also recommends against prescribing pentoxifylline, other anti-inflammatory drugs or letrozole outside ovulation induction to improve natural pregnancy rates (strong, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

NICE describes the evidence on adding hormonal treatment to surgery as mixed (some limited data in favour and some showing no difference), which is why it made a research recommendation. [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.recall: After laparoscopy, when does hormone suppression make sense in a woman who wants to conceive, and when does it not?

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 39 and 40 strong, ⊕⊕; rec. 41 weak, ⊕⊕; rec. 42 strong, ⊕. NICE NG73 1.10.4 [2017, amended 2024].

items.title: Peritoneal disease (rASRM I/II): what treating it at laparoscopy adds
items.core: ESHRE states that operative laparoscopy could be offered for endometriosis-associated infertility in rASRM stage I/II because it improves the ongoing pregnancy rate (weak, ⊕⊕). NICE offers excision or ablation plus adhesiolysis for disease not involving bowel, bladder or ureter, because it improves the chance of spontaneous pregnancy (1.10.1). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
The basis is the 2020 Cochrane review: with moderate-quality evidence from 3 RCTs, laparoscopic surgery increased ultrasound-confirmed viable intrauterine pregnancy compared with diagnostic laparoscopy alone (OR 1.89; 95% CI 1.25–2.86). ESHRE warns that this review found no live-birth data and that a direct comparison with assisted reproduction is lacking. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

ASRM (2012) calculated from two RCTs an absolute difference of 8.6% in favour of treatment (NNT 12), but estimated that in asymptomatic women with otherwise unexplained infertility about 40 laparoscopies would be needed for one additional pregnancy. It concluded the benefit is not enough to recommend laparoscopy for that purpose alone, although visible lesions may be treated if surgery is done for another reason. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]
items.recall: Which outcome does surgery for stage I/II endometriosis improve according to the Cochrane review cited by ESHRE, and which data are missing?
items.pearl: The useful question is not “should I operate to improve fertility?” but “if I am already in, do I treat what I see?”.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022, rec. 43: weak, ⊕⊕. NICE NG73 1.10.1 [2017]. ASRM 2012.

items.title: Endometrioma surgery and ovarian reserve
items.core: ESHRE states that operative laparoscopy may be considered for endometrioma-associated infertility because it may increase natural pregnancy, although no comparative studies exist (weak, ⊕), and calls for specific caution to minimise ovarian damage (strong, ⊕). NICE offers cystectomy with excision of the cyst wall or drainage and ablation, taking into account the possible impact on ovarian reserve and that drainage and ablation may preserve it more than cystectomy (1.10.2). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
In its rationale, NICE found no important difference in pregnancy between cystectomy and drainage with ablation for endometriomas larger than 3 cm, but drainage and ablation may leave more reserve (AMH, ovarian volume and antral follicle count). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

ESHRE reports a 2.4% risk of ovarian failure described after removal of bilateral endometriomas; a prospective study showing greater damage from surgery for recurrent endometriomas than from first surgery; and a meta-analysis confirming that cystectomy, especially for bilateral endometriomas, has a deleterious and sustained effect on ovarian reserve. To prevent pain recurrence it prefers cystectomy over drainage and electrocoagulation, but asks that the reduction in reserve be taken into account (strong, ⊕⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: Which two techniques does NICE offer for endometrioma when pregnancy is sought, and which may preserve reserve better?
items.pearl: Before operating on an endometrioma in someone trying to conceive, be clear what the surgery is for: pain, spontaneous pregnancy or access during IVF.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 44 weak, ⊕; rec. 28 strong, ⊕; rec. 64 strong, ⊕⊕. NICE NG73 1.10.2 [2017, amended 2024].

items.title: Deep endometriosis: wait, operate or move to assisted reproduction
items.core: ESHRE: although there is no compelling evidence that surgery for deep endometriosis improves fertility, it may be an option in symptomatic patients wishing to conceive (weak, ⊕). The decision to operate should be guided by pain, age and preferences, previous surgery, other infertility factors, ovarian reserve and the estimated EFI (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
NICE NG73 asks to discuss with people who have deep endometriosis and are trying to conceive the benefits and risks of surgery, including its possible effect on future pregnancy, the impact on fertility if complications arise, alternatives and other fertility factors (1.10.3), and to refer to a specialist centre (1.5.6). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

NICE NG257, for endometriosis in general, suggests discussing expectant management for up to 2 years (including time already spent trying) or surgical treatment; if there is no pregnancy or these are not appropriate, consider up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophin stimulation before IVF, if appropriate, or offer IVF, taking into account time trying to conceive, symptoms and severity, age, ovarian reserve and male factor (1.36.1–1.36.3). In its rationale, the committee clarifies that in practice IUI with stimulation would suit people without deep endometriosis and with patent tubes. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

ASRM (2012) added that in stage III/IV with previous infertility surgery, IVF is often a better option than reoperation, although this has not been studied in randomised trials. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]
items.recall: Which factors does ESHRE list to decide whether to operate on a woman with endometriosis who is trying to conceive?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 45 weak, ⊕; rec. 46 GPP. NICE NG73 1.10.3 [2017, amended 2024]; NICE NG257 1.36 [2026]. ASRM 2012 (no RCTs on this point).

items.stem: After laparoscopic excision of rASRM stage II endometriosis, a 30-year-old woman wants to try to conceive now. She is offered 6 months of GnRH agonist “to consolidate the surgery”. What is most appropriate?

options.text: Accept: postoperative suppression improves the pregnancy rate.
options.why: ESHRE recommends against postoperative suppression solely to enhance pregnancy (strong, ⊕⊕).

options.text: Try to conceive (or proceed with the indicated fertility treatment) without hormone suppression.
options.why: Correct: neither ESHRE nor NICE supports hormonal treatment, alone or after surgery, in someone trying to conceive.

options.text: Switch to a progestogen for 6 months, which does not inhibit ovulation.
options.why: ASRM (2012) notes that all medical treatments for endometriosis inhibit ovulation; the problem is the same.

options.text: Prescribe continuous letrozole, outside ovulation induction, as an anti-oestrogen.
options.why: ESHRE recommends against letrozole outside ovulation induction to improve natural pregnancy (strong, ⊕).

items.explanation: Hormone suppression after surgery makes sense only if the woman will not try to conceive soon; for someone trying to conceive, it only delays.

items.stem: At a laparoscopy for pelvic pain in a woman with 18 months of infertility, rASRM stage I peritoneal endometriosis lesions are found, without bowel, bladder or ureter involvement. What do the guidelines support?

options.text: Excise or ablate the visible lesions during the same procedure.
options.why: Correct: NICE offers it because it improves spontaneous pregnancy, ESHRE suggests it in stage I/II (weak, ⊕⊕), and ASRM (2012) accepts treating visible disease if laparoscopy is done for another reason.

options.text: Take a biopsy only and treat afterwards with hormone suppression.
options.why: Suppression does not improve fertility (ESHRE, strong, ⊕⊕; NICE 1.10.4) and the opportunity to treat the lesions is lost.

options.text: Leave them: surgery does not change pregnancy in mild disease.
options.why: The Cochrane review cited by ESHRE shows more viable intrauterine pregnancy with surgery (OR 1.89).

options.text: Based on this case, recommend laparoscopy for every woman with unexplained infertility to look for lesions.
options.why: ASRM (2012) estimates about 40 laparoscopies per additional pregnancy in asymptomatic women and considers the benefit insufficient to recommend it for that purpose alone.

items.explanation: If surgery is already under way, treating visible peritoneal disease is supported; looking for it with a laparoscopy done only for infertility is not.

items.stem: A 32-year-old woman with a 5-cm unilateral endometrioma and pain wants to try for a spontaneous pregnancy and opts for surgery. According to NICE NG73, what should be offered?

options.text: Laparoscopic cystectomy or drainage and ablation, explaining that drainage and ablation may preserve ovarian reserve more.
options.why: Correct: this is recommendation 1.10.2; NICE found no important difference in pregnancy between the two techniques.

options.text: Simple drainage, without ablation or excision of the wall.
options.why: NICE refers to drainage with ablation, and ASRM (2012) advised resection or ablation rather than drainage.

options.text: Cystectomy, explaining that in expert hands it does not affect ovarian reserve.
options.why: ESHRE calls for specific caution to minimise ovarian damage and reports a deleterious, sustained effect of cystectomy on reserve.

options.text: Either technique, followed by 6 months of hormone suppression to improve pregnancy.
options.why: NICE 1.10.4 and ESHRE advise against hormonal treatment after surgery in someone trying to conceive.

items.explanation: For endometrioma, the technique is chosen with both pregnancy and the remaining ovarian reserve in mind.

items.title: IUI with stimulation: an option in mild disease
items.core: ESHRE: in rASRM stage I/II, IUI with ovarian stimulation may be used instead of expectant management or IUI alone, because it increases pregnancy rates (weak, ⊕); in stage III/IV with tubal patency its value is uncertain, but it could be considered (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] NICE NG257 suggests that, if there is no pregnancy after up to 2 years of expectant management or after surgery, or if these are not appropriate, up to 4 cycles of IUI with gonadotrophin stimulation be considered before IVF, if appropriate, or IVF be offered (1.36.2). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
ESHRE adds that it may be considered within 6 months after surgery for stage I/II endometriosis, with pregnancy rates similar to those in unexplained infertility. Studies in endometriosis mostly used gonadotrophins; clomiphene and letrozole for IUI have not been studied in endometriosis, and there is only indirect evidence from unexplained infertility. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

In 2012 (before ESHRE 2022 and NICE NG257), ASRM suggested expectant management or IUI with stimulation as first line for women under 35 with stage I/II, and IUI with stimulation or IVF from age 35. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]
items.recall: In which stage and with which type of stimulation does ESHRE support IUI in endometriosis?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 47 and 48 weak, ⊕. NICE NG257 1.36.2 [2026]. ASRM 2012.

items.title: IVF in endometriosis: indications, protocol and safety
items.core: ESHRE: ART can be performed for endometriosis-associated infertility, especially if tubal function is compromised, there is male factor, the EFI is low or other treatments have failed (weak, ⊕⊕). It does not recommend a specific protocol: GnRH antagonist or agonist according to preferences, as no difference in pregnancy or live birth has been shown (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
In the meta-analysis cited by ESHRE, the live-birth rate with stage I/II endometriosis did not differ from that of women without endometriosis (OR 0.96; 95% CI 0.82–1.12), whereas in stage III/IV it was lower (OR 0.77; 95% CI 0.64–0.92), with fewer oocytes and fewer pregnancies. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

On safety, ESHRE allows reassurance: ART does not increase recurrence (weak, ⊕⊕⊕). With an endometrioma, antibiotic prophylaxis may be used at oocyte retrieval, although the risk of ovarian abscess is low (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: In which situations does ESHRE point to ART for endometriosis-associated infertility, and which protocol does it recommend?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 49 weak, ⊕⊕; rec. 50 weak, ⊕; rec. 51 weak, ⊕⊕⊕; rec. 52 GPP.

items.title: Extended GnRH agonist before IVF: what changed
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend extended GnRH agonist administration before ART to improve live birth, because the benefit is uncertain (strong, ⊕), and considers the evidence insufficient for prolonged pre-treatment with combined oral contraceptives or progestogens (weak, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
According to ESHRE, an older Cochrane review (3 studies, 228 patients) suggested that 3–6 months of agonist increased the odds of clinical pregnancy more than 4-fold; its update (8 RCTs, 640 participants) concluded that the effect on live birth and secondary outcomes is very uncertain, with very low-quality data. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

ASRM 2012 cited that earlier summary of 3 RCTs (165 women according to ASRM; ESHRE reports 228 patients; OR 4.28 for clinical pregnancy), while already warning that it was hard to extrapolate given the very high pregnancy rates in the treated arms. It is an example of a recommendation that changes when the evidence is updated. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE recommend about extended GnRH agonist before IVF, and why does it differ from what ASRM cited in 2012?

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 53 strong, ⊕; rec. 54 weak, ⊕. ASRM 2012 predates the Cochrane update.

items.title: Surgery before IVF: not as routine
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend routine surgery before ART to improve live birth in rASRM stage I/II, because the benefit is unclear (strong, ⊕⊕), or removal of an endometrioma, because it shows no benefit and probably reduces ovarian reserve (strong, ⊕⊕); endometrioma surgery may be considered for pain or to improve follicle access (GPP). In deep endometriosis, the decision to operate before ART should be guided mainly by pain and preferences, because its reproductive effect is uncertain (strong, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
In the meta-analyses reported by ESHRE, endometrioma surgery before ART did not change live birth (OR 1.08; 95% CI 0.80–1.45; 7 studies), reduced antral follicle count and increased the FSH dose required; the operated ovary yielded fewer oocytes than the contralateral one. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

ASRM 2012 also considered the evidence insufficient that removing an endometrioma improves IVF, but suggested considering surgery if it is larger than 4 cm, to confirm the diagnosis, improve follicle access and possibly response, warning of possible ovarian damage. [[ref:asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility]]
items.recall: With an asymptomatic endometrioma before IVF, what does ESHRE recommend, and in which two situations may surgery be considered?

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 55 and 56 strong, ⊕⊕; rec. 57 GPP; rec. 58 strong, ⊕. ASRM 2012.

items.title: Fertility preservation: a required conversation, an uncertain benefit
items.core: ESHRE recommends discussing the pros and cons of fertility preservation with women with extensive ovarian endometriosis, and acknowledges that its true benefit in endometriosis is unknown (strong, ⊕). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.body:
ESHRE notes that severe endometriosis, particularly with bilateral endometriomas, carries a high risk of premature ovarian insufficiency and lower AMH, and that surgery can reduce reserve further; the value of pre-treatment AMH to predict pregnancy or the need for preservation is unclear. It cites the ESHRE fertility preservation guideline: if AMH is measured, it should be assessed after surgery. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

In Cobo’s retrospective series (485 patients with endometrioma), oocyte survival after warming was 83.2% and cumulative live birth 46.4%; ESHRE cautions that many used their oocytes early, as part of infertility treatment, and that there are no criteria to select who benefits. Moreover, oocyte cryopreservation is expensive and carries some clinical risks. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE recommend on fertility preservation in extensive ovarian endometriosis, and what remains unknown?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 59 strong, ⊕ (strong for counselling and information, not for preserving in everyone).

items.title: Diet, supplements and complementary therapies: no evidence for fertility
items.core: ESHRE states there is no clear evidence that any non-medical intervention increases pregnancy in women with endometriosis and that none can be recommended (nutrition, Chinese medicine, electrotherapy, acupuncture, physiotherapy, exercise or psychological interventions), because their benefits and harms are unclear (GDG statement). NICE advises that the evidence does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1). [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]
items.body:
ESHRE found only small, low-quality studies: a trial of vitamins C and E versus placebo measured oxidative stress markers and did not increase pregnancy, and a Chinese trial of herbal formulas after surgery showed more live births (34.7% vs 20.8%), but with concepts and compositions hard to apply outside that setting. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

No specific non-medical intervention can be recommended for pain either, although ESHRE acknowledges that many patients seek complementary ways of managing and calls for well-designed trials. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]
items.recall: What do ESHRE and NICE say about nutrition, supplements or acupuncture to improve fertility in endometriosis?
items.pearl: “No evidence” is not the same as “forbidden”: discuss cost and safety, and do not let any of it delay the reproductive plan.

evidence.label: insufficient
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: GDG statement (ungraded), based on small low-quality studies. NICE NG73 1.8.1 [2017].

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman had surgery 3 months ago for rASRM stage II endometriosis; her tubes are patent and her partner’s semen analysis is normal. She has not conceived. Which option does ESHRE support?

options.text: IUI with ovarian stimulation.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE suggests it in stage I/II over expectant management or IUI alone (weak, ⊕), and within 6 months after surgery pregnancy rates are similar to those in unexplained infertility.

options.text: Natural-cycle IUI, preferable to stimulated IUI.
options.why: ESHRE prefers IUI with stimulation over IUI alone because it increases pregnancy.

options.text: 3 to 6 months of GnRH agonist before IUI.
options.why: ESHRE considers it cannot be recommended because of the low IUI success after such prolonged treatment and the side effects.

options.text: Pentoxifylline to improve natural pregnancy.
options.why: ESHRE recommends against pentoxifylline or other anti-inflammatory drugs for that purpose (strong, ⊕).

items.explanation: After treating mild endometriosis, IUI with stimulation is a reasonable option with limited evidence, better than adding unsupported drugs.

items.stem: A 34-year-old woman is about to start IVF. She has a 35-mm left endometrioma without significant pain, and the follicles are accessible on ultrasound. What does ESHRE recommend?

options.text: Remove the endometrioma before IVF to improve live birth.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend it routinely (strong, ⊕⊕): there is no live-birth benefit and it probably reduces reserve.

options.text: Proceed to IVF without prior surgery; consider surgery only for pain or problems accessing the follicles.
options.why: Correct: recommendation 56 (strong, ⊕⊕) and good practice point 57.

options.text: Routinely drain the cyst transvaginally before stimulation.
options.why: ESHRE does not support routine intervention on the endometrioma before ART: it recommends against routine surgery (strong, ⊕⊕) and only reports small studies on aspiration or sclerotherapy, without recommending them.

options.text: Delay IVF for 6 months with contraceptives to shrink the cyst.
options.why: ESHRE considers the evidence insufficient for prolonged pre-treatment with contraceptives or progestogens (weak, ⊕).

items.explanation: Before IVF, an endometrioma is operated on for a specific reason (pain or access), not as routine. ASRM 2012 was somewhat more permissive for cysts larger than 4 cm.

items.stem: A colleague proposes 3 months of GnRH agonist before IVF in a woman with endometriosis, citing a review showing a 4-fold increase in clinical pregnancy. Which answer best matches ESHRE 2022?

options.text: That is right: the evidence is robust and ESHRE recommends it.
options.why: ESHRE recommends against it (strong, ⊕).

options.text: ESHRE does not recommend it: the updated Cochrane review judges the effect on live birth very uncertain.
options.why: Correct: the update (8 RCTs, 640 participants) did not confirm the benefit of the older version, with very low-quality data.

options.text: Better 3 months of combined contraceptive, whose benefit is proven.
options.why: ESHRE considers the evidence insufficient for prolonged pre-treatment with contraceptives or progestogens.

options.text: The long agonist protocol is mandatory in endometriosis.
options.why: ESHRE recommends no specific protocol: antagonist or agonist according to preferences (weak, ⊕).

items.explanation: The “×4” figure comes from an older review of 3 studies; its update and ESHRE 2022 leave it without support for live birth.

items.stem: A patient with endometriosis about to start IVF asks whether an anti-inflammatory diet, vitamins C and E and acupuncture will improve her chances. Which statement is correct?

options.text: ESHRE recommends antioxidant vitamins because they increase pregnancy.
options.why: The vitamin C and E trial reported by ESHRE did not increase pregnancy.

options.text: No non-medical intervention can be recommended to increase fertility; benefits and harms are unclear.
options.why: Correct: this is the ESHRE guideline group statement covering nutrition, Chinese medicine, acupuncture and other interventions.

options.text: NICE recommends Chinese herbal medicine as an adjunct.
options.why: NICE states the evidence does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis.

options.text: IVF should be postponed for 3 months to complete the diet first.
options.why: None of these guidelines supports diet to improve fertility, so it does not justify delaying treatment.

items.explanation: Given the lack of evidence, the honest message is “we do not know whether it helps”: no promises, no bans and no delay to the plan.

items.title: Case: Elena, Raúl and the cyst that did not need removing

steps.text: Elena (fictional case), 34, has had severe dysmenorrhoea for years and deep dyspareunia; Raúl, 36. They have been trying to conceive for 14 months and pelvic examination is normal. Her GP suggests a combined contraceptive as an empirical trial. ESHRE frames empirical treatment for those not trying to conceive, and NICE considers it inappropriate when trying to conceive. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Transvaginal ultrasound shows a 35-mm left endometrioma with no signs of deep disease. She is referred to a specialist endometriosis unit, as NICE advises for an endometrioma (1.5.6). [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]] Raúl’s semen analysis is normal and the tubes are patent. Options are discussed: expectant management, surgery, IUI with stimulation or IVF, taking into account time trying, symptoms, age, ovarian reserve and male factor. [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]

Elena prioritises pregnancy and her pain is controlled with analgesics. The options are reviewed: continue expectant management up to 2 years in total, surgery for the endometrioma (with its possible effect on ovarian reserve) or assisted reproduction. After weighing age, ovarian reserve and preferences, as ESHRE asks when deciding on surgery, Elena prefers neither surgery nor further waiting, and they decide on IVF. Elena asks whether the cyst should be removed first. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
Another clinician suggests 3 months of GnRH agonist before stimulation. ESHRE does not recommend it because the live-birth benefit is uncertain. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Stimulation: an antagonist protocol is chosen by preference, as ESHRE recommends none in particular, and antibiotic prophylaxis at oocyte retrieval is considered because of the endometrioma (GPP). Elena is told that ART does not increase endometriosis recurrence. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]]

Before starting, Elena asks about an anti-inflammatory diet and supplements. It is explained that neither ESHRE nor NICE supports non-medical interventions or supplements to improve fertility or treat endometriosis, and that none of it should delay IVF. [[ref:eshre-2022-endometriosis]] [[ref:nice-2024-ng73]]

asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility.title: Endometriosis and infertility: a committee opinion
asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility.authors: Practice Committee of the American Society for Reproductive Medicine
asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility.population: Committee opinion (Fertil Steril 2012;98:591–8) on infertile women with endometriosis: diagnosis, medical and surgical treatment, IUI with stimulation and IVF. Replaces the 2006 document.
asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility.finding: No evidence that medical treatment improves fertility; all medical treatments inhibit ovulation. In stage I/II, ablation or resection of visible lesions gives an absolute difference of 8.6% in favour (95% CI 2.1–15; NNT 12), but about 40 laparoscopies would be needed for one additional pregnancy in asymptomatic women with otherwise unexplained infertility; the benefit is insufficient to recommend laparoscopy solely to increase the chance of pregnancy. Under 35 with stage I/II: expectant management or stimulation with IUI; 35 or older: IUI with stimulation or IVF. Stage III/IV: conservative surgery may be beneficial; IVF as an effective alternative if no pregnancy after surgery or because of age. Insufficient evidence that removing an endometrioma before IVF improves outcomes; if >4 cm, consider surgery to confirm the diagnosis, improve follicle access and possibly response, warning of possible ovarian damage. Cites a summary of 3 RCTs (165 women) with OR 4.28 for clinical pregnancy with a GnRH agonist for 3–6 months before IVF/ICSI, hard to extrapolate.
asrm-2012-endometriosis-infertility.limitations: 2012 document (full 8-page PDF read). It predates the ESHRE 2022 guideline and the updated Cochrane review on GnRH agonist before IVF, which ESHRE judges very uncertain; on that point and on endometrioma surgery before IVF, ESHRE is more restrictive. Whether a newer ASRM version exists was not checked in the ASRM listing.

eshre-2022-endometriosis.title: ESHRE guideline: endometriosis (full guideline)
eshre-2022-endometriosis.authors: ESHRE Endometriosis Guideline Development Group (Becker CM, Bokor A, Heikinheimo O, Horne A, Jansen F, Kiesel L, King K, Kvaskoff M, Nap A, Petersen K, et al.)
eshre-2022-endometriosis.population: Women with diagnosed or strongly suspected endometriosis; includes chapters on pain, infertility, recurrence, adolescence and menopause. Does not cover adenomyosis. Literature search up to 1 Dec 2020. Full 192-page guideline; recommendations labelled strong or weak (GRADE) with their level of evidence (⊕ symbols), plus good practice points (GPP) and guideline group (GDG) statements.
eshre-2022-endometriosis.finding: Diagnosis: use imaging (ultrasound or MRI), aware that a negative result does not exclude it, particularly superficial peritoneal disease (rec. 5, strong, ⊕⊕); do not use biomarkers (rec. 4, strong, ⊕⊕⊕); diagnostic laparoscopy or imaging plus empirical treatment, with no proven superiority of either (GDG statement); empirical treatment is considered if the patient is not trying to conceive. Infertility: do not prescribe ovarian suppression to improve fertility (rec. 39, strong, ⊕⊕) or postoperative suppression solely to enhance pregnancy rates (rec. 40, strong, ⊕⊕); operative laparoscopy in rASRM stage I/II (rec. 43, weak, ⊕⊕); for endometrioma (rec. 44, weak, ⊕) and deep disease (rec. 45, weak, ⊕); use the EFI to identify who benefits from ART after surgery (GDG statement); IUI with ovarian stimulation in stage I/II (rec. 47, weak, ⊕); ART if tubal or male factor, low EFI or failed other treatments (rec. 49, weak, ⊕⊕); no preferred protocol (rec. 50, weak, ⊕); no extended GnRH agonist before ART (rec. 53, strong, ⊕); insufficient evidence for COC/progestogen pre-treatment (rec. 54, weak, ⊕); no routine surgery before ART in stage I/II (rec. 55, strong, ⊕⊕) or for endometrioma (rec. 56, strong, ⊕⊕); endometrioma surgery before ART for pain or follicle access (rec. 57, GPP); fertility preservation: discuss pros and cons with extensive ovarian endometriosis (rec. 59, strong, ⊕); no non-medical intervention (nutrition, Chinese medicine, acupuncture, etc.) can be recommended to increase fertility (GDG statement).
eshre-2022-endometriosis.limitations: Read in the full guideline: the list of recommendations (pp. 9–14), sections I.2.b–I.2.c, II.3.e (ovarian reserve) and III.1–III.8. The guideline produced no GRADE summary-of-findings tables because evidence was insufficient; most infertility recommendations rest on ⊕ or ⊕⊕ evidence and several are GPPs (expert opinion). Level of evidence per Annex 4: ⊕ very low, ⊕⊕ low, ⊕⊕⊕ moderate, ⊕⊕⊕⊕ high; a recommendation can be strong with ⊕ evidence. Surgical studies were not stratified by EFI. Search closed in 2020; whether a later update exists was not checked.

nice-2024-ng73.title: Endometriosis: diagnosis and management (NG73)
nice-2024-ng73.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2024-ng73.population: Women and people with suspected or confirmed endometriosis, including those aged 17 and under, in the English health system. Published 6 Sep 2017; last updated 11 Nov 2024. Each recommendation carries the year it was written or changed ([2017], [2024], [2017, amended 2024]); NICE does not attach GRADE grades in the recommendation text.
nice-2024-ng73.finding: Offer transvaginal ultrasound to anyone with suspected endometriosis even if examination is normal (1.5.2); do not exclude endometriosis if examination and ultrasound are normal (1.5.4); do not use CA125 to diagnose it (1.5.8); consider specialist ultrasound or MRI for deep disease (1.5.9) and laparoscopy even if imaging is normal (1.5.11); refer to a specialist centre for endometrioma or deep disease (1.5.6); treat according to symptoms, preferences and priorities rather than stage (1.6.1). When fertility is a priority: offer excision or ablation plus adhesiolysis for disease not involving bowel, bladder or ureter (1.10.1); offer laparoscopic cystectomy or drainage and ablation of endometriomas, taking into account that drainage and ablation may preserve ovarian reserve more (1.10.2); discuss benefits and risks of surgery for deep endometriosis (1.10.3); do not offer hormonal treatment alone or with surgery to people trying to conceive (1.10.4). Does not support traditional Chinese medicine, other herbal medicines or supplements for treating endometriosis (1.8.1).
nice-2024-ng73.limitations: Read sections 1.5–1.10, the rationale for 1.10.2–1.10.4 and the context (full PDF, 33 pp.). The fertility recommendations are to be read alongside NICE NG257; the evidence on hormonal treatment combined with surgery is described as mixed. Evidence reviews A and B were not read. Guideline designed for the English health system.

nice-2026-ng257.title: Fertility problems: assessment and treatment (NG257)
nice-2026-ng257.authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
nice-2026-ng257.population: People with fertility problems in the UK health system.
nice-2026-ng257.finding: Do not use AMH to predict clinical pregnancy through spontaneous conception (1.18.3). Use AMH or AFC as predictors of ovarian response to inform decisions and counselling about the likelihood of live birth after assisted conception (1.18.4). Do not use FSH as a predictor (1.18.5). Refer at presentation if the woman is 36 or over or there is a known cause or predisposing factors (1.16.8); otherwise investigation after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.
nice-2026-ng257.limitations: NHS (UK) context; replaces CG156. Numbering checked in the March 2026 PDF.
